title: Remarks on Antwerp's apology for the 1942 deportation of Jews
description: In October 2007 Antwerp mayor Patrick Janssens apologised on behalf of the city for its role in the three round-ups of 1942, which led to the deportation of about 1,200 Jewish residents via Mechelen to Auschwitz (La Libre). De Wever, then N-VA chairman and a city councillor, told De Standaard that the apology was "gratuitous" and aimed at fighting Vlaams Belang, and said, as quoted by La Libre: "It was not the city of Antwerp that organised the deportation; it was itself a victim of the occupation. Those who ran it had to take delicate decisions in difficult circumstances. I do not find it very courageous to stigmatise them now." He also referred to the occupied Palestinian territories, where he said some used techniques that reminded him of a dark past. The remarks were criticised by representatives of Antwerp's Jewish community and by Open VLD, while historical research had documented the involvement of the Antwerp police and city administration in the round-ups. After meeting representatives of the Forum der Joodse Organisaties, De Wever apologised for what he called an error of judgement. In a December 2007 article in Le Monde the writer Pierre Mertens called him a "negationist"; De Wever filed a defamation complaint against Mertens (Wikipedia), whose outcome could not be confirmed for this profile.
key_facts: De Wever called Janssens' October 2007 apology "gratuitous" and said the city had itself been a victim of the occupation (La Libre, 30 October 2007)
He later apologised to representatives of the Jewish community for an error of judgement
He filed a defamation complaint against writer Pierre Mertens over a Le Monde article calling him a negationist; outcome not confirmed

title: Der Spiegel interview calling Belgium "the sick man of Europe"
description: In December 2010, during the record-length government formation that followed the June 2010 election, De Wever gave an interview to the German weekly Der Spiegel in which he called Belgium "the sick man of Europe" and, according to La Libre, accused the King of not being impartial; the Dutch-language Wikipedia reports he called the King "not important". The interview drew criticism because it came at a sensitive moment in the negotiations on a state reform. Carine Doutrelepont, a media-law lecturer at the ULB, argued in Le Soir that the remarks could amount to press offences (offence to the person of the King and undermining the credit of the State), and a Tournai resident, Georges Oldenhove de Guertechin, filed a complaint with the local police on those grounds. La Libre reported in January 2011 that he had heard nothing about its follow-up; no prosecution has been reported.
key_facts: Der Spiegel interview, December 2010, during the 2010–2011 formation crisis
A citizen's complaint for offence to the King and undermining the credit of the State was filed with the police (La Libre, 24 January 2011)
No prosecution reported

title: Remarks on racism and the Berber community (Terzake, March 2015)
description: On VRT's Terzake programme in March 2015, De Wever, then N-VA chairman and Mayor of Antwerp, said that Belgium had "allowed the wrong kind of migrants to come en masse and then too little was done", described racism as a "relative" notion too often invoked as an excuse for personal failure, and said: "Especially the Berbers. These are closed communities, with distrust of the authorities" (as quoted by RTBF). Councillors from CD&V and Groen criticised the remarks and Groen's Wouter Van Besien asked him to apologise in the Antwerp city council, which he declined to do (La Libre). A lawyer, Abderrahim Lahlali, acting for the Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH), Dyab Abou Jahjah's Movement X and nine citizens filed complaints for racism. The Antwerp prosecutor's office dismissed the AMDH complaint, finding no offence; see the justice section. De Wever said the decision confirmed that "explaining facts is not an offence".
key_facts: Remarks made on VRT's Terzake in March 2015
De Wever refused to apologise in the Antwerp city council (La Libre, 31 March 2015)
Racism complaints filed; the Antwerp prosecutor dismissed the AMDH complaint (reported August 2016)

title: N-VA leaves the Michel government over the UN migration pact
description: In late 2018 the N-VA, then a member of Prime Minister Charles Michel's 'Swedish' coalition, turned against the UN Global Compact for Migration, which Michel had endorsed at the UN in September 2018. According to RTBF, the party ran a social-media campaign against the pact using stock photos taken out of context, which Vlaams Belang MP Filip Dewinter praised. After the Chamber adopted a resolution supporting the pact, De Wever said that if Michel went to Marrakesh to approve it, the N-VA would consider itself "dismissed from the government" and Michel would "land as Prime Minister of the Marrakesh coalition". On 8 December 2018 Michel took note that the N-VA had left the government; the minority government later resigned and stayed on as a caretaker government. RTBF notes that the N-VA lost ground in the May 2019 elections while Vlaams Belang advanced.
key_facts: 8 December 2018: extraordinary cabinet meeting fails to reach consensus; Michel takes note of the N-VA's departure
De Wever: Michel would become "Prime Minister of the Marrakesh coalition"
N-VA fell below 30% in Flanders in May 2019 (RTBF)

title: Talks with Vlaams Belang after the 2019 Flemish election
description: After the 26 May 2019 elections, in which Vlaams Belang became Flanders' second party, De Wever said the N-VA had "never subscribed" to the cordon sanitaire, while objecting to some of that party's positions, style and figures (VRT). As informateur for the Flemish government he then held talks with Vlaams Belang until 12 August 2019, when he concluded that a government with the party was impossible because no other party would join it, and presented a starting note for a coalition of N-VA, CD&V and Open VLD; Jan Jambon then led the negotiations and became Minister-President. VRT wrote that the note met several of Vlaams Belang's wishes on integration and identity (a compulsory citizenship test, a five-year legal residence condition for some Flemish benefits), while Vlaams Belang called the result a "coalition of losers". Groen leader Meyrem Almaci said De Wever had "written a starting note together with Vlaams Belang". In August 2019 De Wever said on Terzake that there was a "Chinese wall" between the two parties that he would "never" cross (RTBF).
key_facts: De Wever: the N-VA "never subscribed" to the cordon sanitaire (VRT, 26 May 2019)
12 August 2019: talks with Vlaams Belang ended; starting note for N-VA, CD&V and Open VLD
Groen's Almaci: the note was written "together with Vlaams Belang" (VRT, 25 August 2019)

title: Doubts on whether Belgium would arrest Netanyahu under the ICC warrant
description: Asked on VRT's Terzake on 3 April 2025 about Hungary's refusal to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, De Wever said he understood the decision: "And I think we would not do it either, to be quite honest... There is also realpolitik. I think no European state would arrest Netanyahu if he were on its territory", while criticising Hungary's withdrawal from the ICC (RTBF). Groen said the Prime Minister was placing Belgium "outside the international order", Open VLD spoke of a "flagrant disregard of international law" and PVDA-PTB also criticised him; MP Fouad Ahidar called for his resignation, while MR chairman Georges-Louis Bouchez backed him (La Libre). Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot had told the Chamber on 26 February 2025 that Belgium would comply with the warrant if necessary, and a law professor quoted by RTBF said it was unclear whether such warrants bind leaders of states not party to the ICC. On 9 April 2025 Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden (CD&V) told the Chamber that Belgium, as a state party, is legally obliged to execute the Court's arrest and surrender requests and saw "no reason" to change its cooperation with the Court.
key_facts: Remarks on Terzake, 3 April 2025
Criticism from Groen, Open VLD, PVDA-PTB and Fouad Ahidar; support from MR chairman Bouchez
Justice Minister Verlinden: Belgium is legally obliged to execute ICC arrest requests (VRT, 9 April 2025)

title: Critic's e-mail forwarded to the police
description: Walter Nauwelaerts, a retired teacher and CD&V member from Hoboken, sent De Wever several angry e-mails about the government's Gaza policy; in the last one he referred to the Prime Minister's "backward Orthodox-Jewish base". According to VRT, De Wever forwarded that e-mail to the police because he considered it antisemitic, and Nauwelaerts was then invited to a police interview on suspicion of harassment, incitement to discrimination, hatred and violence, and nuisance by electronic communication; VRT reported that the police themselves added the harassment element because of the number of e-mails. Nauwelaerts acknowledged the wording was "not pretty" but invoked freedom of expression; emeritus media-law professor Dirk Voorhoof (UGent) criticised the use of criminal law against critics of government leaders, and CD&V chairman Sammy Mahdi said the case had "the appearance of political intimidation". De Wever's spokesman called that accusation "complete nonsense" and said no criminal complaint had ever been filed against anyone; VRT described it as a report to the police rather than a complaint. No outcome of the police inquiry has been reported.
key_facts: De Wever forwarded the e-mail to the police as antisemitic (VRT, 15 September 2025)
Mahdi (CD&V): "appearance of political intimidation"; De Wever's spokesman: "complete nonsense", no criminal complaint filed
Outcome of the police inquiry not reported

title: Opposition to an EU reparations loan based on Russian assets held at Euroclear
description: Most of the Russian central bank assets frozen in the EU are held by the securities depository Euroclear in Brussels. From September 2025 De Wever opposed the European Commission's plan to use them to fund a 'reparations loan' to Ukraine, citing legal and financial risks for Belgium that he said were not sufficiently shared by other member states; at the October 2025 summit he noted that Japan had ruled out using the Russian reserves it holds. In December 2025 seven member states (Poland, Sweden, Lithuania, Estonia, Finland, Ireland and Latvia) wrote to the EU leadership urging that the plan go ahead, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz travelled to Brussels to discuss Belgium's objections. At the European Council of 18 December 2025 leaders instead agreed a 90-billion-euro loan to Ukraine financed by joint EU borrowing, with the Russian assets remaining frozen; De Wever called it a victory for Ukraine, Europe and financial stability.
key_facts: De Wever rejected Chancellor Merz's proposal to use the frozen assets (VRT, 26 September 2025)
Seven member states pressed for the reparations loan in December 2025
18 December 2025: EU leaders opted for a 90-billion-euro joint loan; Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia obtained an opt-out

title: Repeated budget deadlocks and cancelled State of the Union speeches
description: In October 2025 the Arizona coalition failed to agree on a multi-year budget in time and De Wever's State of the Union address was not delivered; he went to King Philippe, who gave him until Christmas to reach an agreement (VRT). A deal worth 9.2 billion euros a year by 2029 was concluded on 24 November 2025. The scenario repeated itself in 2026: an initial 21 July deadline was dropped, and on 11 October 2026 De Wever cancelled the State of the Union scheduled for 13 October, saying provisional twelfths were not an option given "the seriousness of the budgetary situation and developments on the financial markets". His proposal for a 'stability law' (dubbed a 'debt brake'), an emergency package of about 4 billion euros, was rejected by coalition partners and dropped on 17 October in favour of renewed talks on a 10-billion-euro multi-year budget. CD&V chairman Sammy Mahdi called the debt brake an attack on pensioners' indexation and Anders chairman Frédéric De Gucht criticised De Wever's method; political scientist Dave Sinardet called the situation a "gigantic déjà vu". As of 22 October 2026 there was still no agreement and the 15 October deadline for submitting the budget to the European Commission had passed.
key_facts: 2025: State of the Union not delivered; King Philippe gave De Wever until Christmas; agreement on 24 November 2025
2026: State of the Union of 13 October cancelled; 'debt brake' proposal dropped on 17 October
No 2027–2029 budget agreement as of 22 October 2026

title: Call to normalise relations with Russia to regain cheap energy
description: In an interview with the financial daily L'Echo published on the weekend of 14–15 March 2026, while energy prices were rising because of the war in Iran, De Wever said the European Union should negotiate with Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine and normalise relations with Russia: "That way, we will regain access to cheap energy. That is common sense." He also said Ukraine must remain sovereign and that a truce line should be a fortified border. The remarks ran counter to the EU line of phasing out Russian gas and oil imports (VRT). Coalition partners Vooruit, CD&V and Les Engagés called them "strange", "naive" and "a sign of weakness", the last being Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot's words, while Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said they showed there was still "a bit of common sense" in parts of Europe. De Wever then said his words had been blown out of proportion: a peace treaty acceptable to Ukraine and Europe must come first, and only then could economic relations be restored.
key_facts: L'Echo interview, mid-March 2026
Criticism from coalition partners; welcomed by the Russian Foreign Ministry
De Wever clarified on 16–17 March 2026 that peace must come before any normalisation

title: Trade-union strikes and mass demonstrations against the government's reforms
description: The three main trade unions (ABVV-FGTB, ACV-CSC and ACLVB-CGSLB) have organised repeated actions against the austerity, pension and unemployment-benefit reforms of De Wever's government: a demonstration of 60,000 to 100,000 people in Brussels on 13 February 2025, on 31 March 2025 the first general strike in Belgium in more than ten years, a demonstration of 80,000 (police figure) to 140,000 (union figure) on 14 October 2025, four consecutive days of action at the end of November 2025, a march of about 100,000 people on 12 March 2026 (Dutch-language Wikipedia) and a further national demonstration in Brussels on 9 October 2026 (30,000 people according to the police), marked by violence on its margins (AFP via La Libre). Forty-two emeritus professors criticised what they called the "dismantling of social security" in an open letter, and the participation of the social-democratic Vooruit in the government drew criticism from the unions. The government has maintained its reforms.
key_facts: 31 March 2025: first general strike in more than a decade
14 October 2025: 80,000–140,000 demonstrators in Brussels
9 October 2026: national union demonstration in Brussels against austerity, 30,000 people according to the police
